title: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy
backgroundAndFacts:
Colorado operates a publicly funded childcare assistance program that subsidizes the cost of childcare for low-income families. The program allows families to use these funds at a wide variety of private childcare providers. However, Colorado excludes religious providers — such as St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton — that operate according to religious beliefs and practices, including beliefs about marriage, gender, and sexuality, that conflict with the state's nondiscrimination requirements. St. Mary and other religious providers argue that this exclusion forces them to choose between participating in the program and maintaining their religious identity and mission.

St. Mary Catholic Parish and other petitioners sued Colorado officials, arguing that being shut out of the program simply because they are religious — and because of the content of their religious beliefs — violates the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause and the Constitution's Equal Protection Clause. The federal district court and then the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the religious providers. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, limiting its review to two questions from the petition: whether excluding religious providers from the program violates the Free Exercise Clause and whether it violates equal protection principles.

The case arrives at the Supreme Court amid a series of recent decisions that have expanded religious organizations' rights to participate in government benefit programs on equal footing with secular organizations. The outcome will have significant implications for how states can structure public benefit programs when religious providers wish to participate while maintaining their faith-based policies.
legalQuestion: Whether the Free Exercise and Equal Protection Clauses of the Constitution permit Colorado to exclude religious childcare providers from a publicly funded childcare assistance program solely because of their religious beliefs and practices.
significance:
This case could significantly expand — or clarify the limits of — the Supreme Court's recent line of decisions holding that states cannot categorically exclude religious organizations from public benefit programs. Cases like Espinoza v. Montana and Carson v. Makin established that states may not bar religious schools from scholarship programs solely because of their religious status. Here the Court must decide whether the same principle applies when a religious provider's practices (not just its identity) are the reason for exclusion, and whether states have greater flexibility to exclude providers whose conduct conflicts with anti-discrimination rules.

The decision will affect millions of families across the country who rely on religious childcare providers, as well as the providers themselves. It will also shape how states design social service programs going forward — determining how much room states have to impose nondiscrimination conditions that religious organizations cannot meet. Given the enormous number of amicus briefs filed on both sides, the case has mobilized a broad coalition of religious, civil rights, education, and LGBTQ+ advocacy groups who view the outcome as consequential for the future of both religious liberty and anti-discrimination law.

parties.party: St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, et al.
parties.coreArgument: Colorado's exclusion of religious childcare providers from a publicly funded assistance program violates the Free Exercise Clause because it singles out religious organizations based on their religious beliefs and practices, and it violates equal protection by treating religious providers worse than comparable secular providers. Under recent Supreme Court precedent, the government cannot condition access to generally available public benefits on the surrender of First Amendment rights.
supportingPoints: Under Espinoza v. Montana and Carson v. Makin, states cannot exclude religious providers from public benefit programs open to secular counterparts, regardless of whether the exclusion targets religious status or religious conduct.

Colorado's program is not neutral with respect to religion because it specifically targets the religious beliefs and faith-based practices of providers like St. Mary, triggering strict scrutiny under the Free Exercise Clause.

Colorado cannot satisfy strict scrutiny because it has no compelling interest sufficient to justify denying religious organizations access to a program available to a wide range of other private providers, and it has not chosen the least restrictive means of advancing any such interest.
Excluding religious providers harms not only the providers but also the low-income families who prefer faith-based childcare, effectively penalizing those families for their religious preferences.

parties.coreArgument: Colorado's childcare assistance program applies neutral, generally applicable nondiscrimination requirements to all providers, and religious organizations that decline to comply are not excluded because of their religious identity but because of their discriminatory conduct toward families and children. The state has a compelling interest in ensuring that public funds do not subsidize discrimination against LGBTQ+ families and others protected under state law.
supportingPoints: Prior Supreme Court decisions like Espinoza and Carson addressed exclusions based on religious status; Colorado's exclusion is based on discriminatory conduct, not religious identity, and therefore does not trigger the same constitutional concerns.
States retain authority to impose nondiscrimination conditions on participation in publicly funded programs to protect children, families, and the integrity of public funds.

Requiring Colorado to fund religious providers that discriminate against LGBTQ+ families would effectively compel the government to subsidize discrimination, raising serious Establishment Clause concerns.

The Free Exercise Clause does not require the government to subsidize every religious practice, and the program's neutrally applied conditions do not impose a substantial burden on religion that would require strict scrutiny.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Established that a state cannot exclude religious schools from a generally available scholarship program based solely on their religious status, which petitioners argue controls here.

Extended Espinoza to hold that states cannot exclude religious schools from tuition assistance programs because of the religious content of their instruction, which petitioners argue covers exclusions based on religious conduct as well as status.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Held that excluding a religious organization from a government benefit program open to secular counterparts is presumptively unconstitutional under the Free Exercise Clause.

Held that Philadelphia violated the Free Exercise Clause by refusing to contract with a Catholic foster care agency that declined to certify same-sex couples, relevant here because it addressed the tension between religious exercise and anti-discrimination requirements in government programs.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Established that laws that are not neutral and generally applicable with respect to religion must survive strict scrutiny, which petitioners argue Colorado's exclusion cannot satisfy.

Established the general rule that neutral, generally applicable laws do not violate the Free Exercise Clause even if they incidentally burden religious practice, which respondents invoke to defend Colorado's program conditions.
